summary: Both sides render the same frozen clock picture (dim grey strip, blue marker at index 0, 4-unit red bar beside it), but the port lights one extra pixel of blue (double width at the 60 px native rig), pushes the red bar one pixel right, and gets all three colours slightly wrong; the pattern's actual time behaviour is unverifiable because neither engine responds to --wall-clock.
observations: SUSPECTED ENGINE GAP: neither side reacts to the pinned wall clock. Rendered output is byte-identical at --wall-clock 0, 1, 43200, 1000000000, 1756000000, 1756003600, 1756010000, 1756040000, 1756060000, 1756080000 and 2000000000 (checked by --dump pixel comparison, and meta.json settings.wallClock confirms the flag was recorded). For a pattern plainly meant to display time-of-day, that means the engine's clock builtins are returning constants; the port's time->position mapping therefore could NOT be verified at all, on either side. Everything below describes the single frozen instant both engines happen to show (consistent with hour=minute=second=0).

Both sides are completely static: motion 0 and motionLit 0 on every captured frame at 6 s/20 fps (120 frames), 60 s/5 fps (300 frames) and 240 s/2 fps (480 frames); zeroMotionFrames = all frames on both; brightnessTrend steady on both. meanBrightness is a flat 18 (orig) vs 16 (port) with no drift, and a --skip 300 capture is pixel-identical to t=0, so there is no late-window divergence and no warm-up transient on either side.
Neither side compiles or runs with errors; wantsSensors is false on both, so the sensor feed is irrelevant here.
Control surfaces MATCH: meta.json reports controls: [] on both orig and port; --probe-controls reports '(no settable controls)' for both sides. No dial work was possible or needed.

STRUCTURE at the default 60 px strip (exact --dump values, run-length encoded): orig = px0 (0,51,127) | px1-4 (255,51,51) | px5-59 (10,10,10). port = px0-1 (0,0,127) | px2-5 (255,51,75) | px6-59 (7,7,7).

OFF-BY-ONE, confirmed resolution-independent. Re-rendered at --pixels 300 and --pixels 600 the geometry scales as fractions of the strip on BOTH sides, i.e. both are resolution-independent, but the port is consistently one PIXEL wider on the leading marker: 300 px -> orig blue 0-4 (5 px = 1/60 of strip), red 5-24 (20 px = 4/60), total lit 25 px; port blue 0-5 (6 px), red 6-25 (20 px), total lit 26 px. 600 px -> orig blue 0-9 (10 px), red 10-49 (40 px), total 50 px; port blue 0-10 (11 px), red 11-50 (40 px), total 51 px. So orig marker = pixelCount/60 pixels exactly, port marker = pixelCount/60 + 1. The red bar's WIDTH is identical on both (4 * pixelCount/60); it is simply shifted right by one pixel. At the native 60 px rig this makes the port's blue marker 2 px instead of 1 px - a 100% width error on the most eye-catching feature - and moves the red bar from px1-4 to px2-5.

COLOUR - blue marker: orig (0,51,127) = hsv(0.6, 1, 0.5), a green-tinted azure; port (0,0,127) = hsv(2/3, 1, 0.5), pure blue. Hue is off by ~0.067 (~24 deg). The orig's green component (51 at px0) is the ONLY green outside the red bar; the port has none there.

COLOUR - red bar: orig (255,51,51) = hsv(0, 0.8, 1), a clean red; port (255,51,75), i.e. 24 counts of extra blue, reading as a slightly pink/magenta-leaning red (equivalently a hue ~0.02 below 0, or a red with the blue channel raised from 0.2 to 0.294).

COLOUR - background: orig (10,10,10) uniformly on px5-59; port (7,7,7) on px6-59. The port's idle field is ~30% dimmer. This accounts for most of the whole-strip mean gap (orig meanBrightness 18 / meanR 26 / meanG 13 / meanB 15 vs port 16 / 23 / 10 / 16).

Both sides are INDEX-ONLY, and agree on that: re-rendered on --rig grid --grid 8x8 the flat pixel sequence is identical to the 60 px strip render on each side (orig px0 marker, px1-4 bar, rest background; port px0-1, px2-5, rest), so neither side is (x,y)-driven and the port has not introduced a coordinate dependence.

Small-rig artefact worth flagging, not headline: at --pixels 12 the ORIGINAL floods all 12 pixels with the marker colour (0,51,127) and shows no red bar or background at all (meanBrightness 59), while the port still draws the normal 1 px blue / 1 px red / 10 px background layout (meanBrightness 20). The original apparently degenerates when pixelCount/60 < 1; the port degrades more gracefully. This is off the default rig, so it is a curiosity rather than a port defect, but it is a real behavioural difference at very low pixel counts.
feedback: BLOCKER FOR ANY REAL VERIFICATION: the engine's wall-clock/time-of-day builtins appear to return constants - both the original and the port render byte-identical output across wall clocks spanning 0 to 2000000000 epoch seconds. Until the engine actually surfaces the pinned clock, no clock pattern can be judged on the thing it exists to do. This should be filed as an engine gap, not charged against the port.

Fix the off-by-one on the leading blue marker: the original lights exactly pixelCount/60 pixels (1 px on the 60 px rig, 5 px at 300 px, 10 px at 600 px); the port lights one MORE than that (2 / 6 / 11). The boundary is inclusive in the port where the original's is exclusive. Correcting it also removes the one-pixel rightward shift of the red bar, whose width is already correct (4 * pixelCount/60).

Blue marker hue: original renders (0,51,127) - hsv(0.6, 1, 0.5), an azure with a visible green component. Port renders (0,0,127) - hsv(2/3, 1, 0.5), pure blue. Move the marker hue from 2/3 down to 0.6.

Red bar tint: original is (255,51,51) - a neutral red, hsv(0, 0.8, 1). Port is (255,51,75) - 24 counts of extra blue, reading pink. Drop the bar's blue channel to match the green channel (both 51 = 0.2 of full) so the hue sits at exactly 0.
Background level: original's idle pixels are (10,10,10); the port's are (7,7,7), about 30% dimmer. Raise the background grey by ~40% (0.0275 -> 0.039 of full scale).

Once the clock builtins work, re-verify the thing that actually matters and could not be checked here: that the marker and bar move to the right positions as hours/minutes/seconds advance, and in the same direction and units as the original. Every difference listed above is a static-appearance nitpick; the time mapping is completely untested.
